sections.h2: What should a seller know about Barron County before dealing with property tax?
sections.html:
Barron County sits in northwestern Wisconsin, bordered by Washburn, Sawyer, Rusk, Chippewa, Dunn, St. Croix, Polk and Burnett counties. It covers 890 square miles, with only about 3 percent of that water, and the county seat is the city of Barron. The 2020 census counted 46,711 residents, and about 78 percent lived in rural areas. The county was created in 1859 as Dallas County, renamed Barron County in 1869 and organized in 1874.

The 2020 census listed 23,779 housing units, of which 17.4 percent were vacant, and 73.2 percent of occupied homes were owner-occupied. The incorporated places are the cities of Barron, Chetek, Cumberland and Rice Lake and the villages of Almena, Cameron, Dallas, Haugen, New Auburn, Prairie Farm and Turtle Lake. Those places and the surrounding towns each have a treasurer who collects first-installment payments.

sections.h2: Which Barron County office handles my property tax?
sections.html:
The Barron County Treasurer and Real Property Lister is the county office to know. It sits at 335 E Monroe Ave, Room 2412, Barron, WI 54812-1478, is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday, and answers at 715-537-6280. The Real Property Lister side keeps the parcel descriptions that feed the assessment and tax roll, pulling together records from the Register of Deeds, surveying, zoning and mapping, the assessor and the treasurer. The office also hosts the online tax data portal.

Wisconsin sets the dates by statute. Under Wis. Stat. 74.11, real property tax is paid in full or in two equal installments, with the first due January 31 and the second July 31. A parcel with a total bill under $100 is paid in full by January 31. Payments made on or before January 31 go to the town, village or city treasurer, and later payments go to the county treasurer. Your municipal clerk tells you who assessed your parcel and when the local Board of Review meets, because assessment is local in Wisconsin.

sections.h2: How do late payments work in Barron County?
sections.html:
Interest and penalty run back to February 1. The county posts the rate as 1 percent interest plus a half percent penalty each month, which is 1.5 percent a month and matches the interest authority in Wis. Stat. 74.47. The county lists 10.5 percent as the August charge on 2025 taxes still unpaid after the July 31, 2026 installment date, and notes that 2025 taxes are due in 2026 because taxes follow the prior year's assessment.

Under state law, a late first installment makes the whole unpaid balance delinquent as of February 1. Mail timing deserves attention:

  • A mailed check must be postmarked on or before the due date.
  • The county warns that local mail is often postmarked in Saint Paul, Minnesota, sometimes days later, so take the envelope to the local post office and ask for a hand stamp.
  • Envelopes that arrive with no postmark cannot be treated as timely.

Counties and municipalities can sue an owner to recover delinquent taxes that came due during that owner's period of ownership, normally after the county board or governing body approves, and only up to the amount owed plus interest and penalties, under chapter 74.

sections.h2: What does a Barron County tax bill show, and when does it arrive?
sections.html: State law requires the bill to go out no later than the third Monday in December, and not receiving it does not change what is owed or the collection of delinquent tax. The bill lists the tax from each taxing jurisdiction for the previous and current year with the percentage change, shows the school district tax net of the state credit, includes a notice of available credits, and says whether delinquent taxes or special assessments are attached to the parcel. That last line is worth reading before you list a house, since it is the quickest way to spot a past-due amount. These requirements come from Wis. Stat. 74.09, which sits next to the payment rules in chapter 74.

sections.h2: How can I pay Barron County property tax?
sections.html:
The treasurer accepts four methods, and card and electronic payments carry fees paid by the taxpayer.

sections.h2: What deadlines should a Barron County homeowner or seller watch?
sections.html:
A few small dates cause most of the grief.

  • January 15, land divisions. If the property was split into two or more parcels, the tax roll still shows the land as it existed on January 1. A new owner who wants a bill split for the part they bought must ask the town, village or city treasurer in writing by January 15.
  • January 31, first installment. Pay in full or pay the first half, to the municipal treasurer, to avoid interest and penalty.
  • January 31, lottery and gaming credit. The credit applies to owner-occupied primary residences. If it is missing from your statement and you qualify, file a late claim with the municipal treasurer by this date.
  • July 31, second installment. Late payment adds charges retroactive to February 1.

Assessment objections follow a different clock. Wisconsin requires notice of intent to object at least 48 hours before the first Board of Review meeting and a written objection filed within the first two hours of that meeting, as the Department of Revenue explains. The assessor must mail a notice of a changed assessment at least 15 days before the board meets, or 30 days in a revaluation year. Your municipal clerk posts the meeting date.

sections.h2: What does a Barron County seller owe at closing?
sections.html:
The seller pays Wisconsin's real estate transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value, collected by the register of deeds when the deed is recorded. A $180,000 house therefore carries a $540 fee. The grantor and grantee both sign an electronic transfer return first. The fee statute, Wis. Stat. 77.22, and its exemption list in section 77.25 cover conveyances by will or descent, foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu of foreclosure to the lender and transfers between a parent and child for little or no payment. A conveyance claiming an exemption must state the reason on its face.

Property taxes are a separate item. Ask the Barron County Treasurer for a statement of any delinquent amount on the parcel, and ask your title company how the current year will be split between you and the buyer. Delinquent real property tax can be discharged by paying the amount with interest and any penalty before a tax certificate is issued. Because first-installment payments go to the municipal treasurer, confirm with that treasurer which installment has been paid.

faqs.q: When are Barron County property taxes due?
faqs.a: January 31 for the first installment or the full bill, and July 31 for the second installment. A bill under $100 is paid in full by January 31. Payments by January 31 go to your town, village or city treasurer.

faqs.q: What interest applies to late Barron County taxes?
faqs.a: 1.5 percent per month, calculated back to February 1: 1 percent interest plus a half percent penalty. The county gives 10.5 percent as the August figure for 2025 taxes.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Barron County Treasurer?
faqs.a: Call 715-537-6280 or visit Room 2412 at 335 E Monroe Ave in Barron, Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mail goes to Barron County Treasurer's Office, 335 E Monroe Ave Rm 2412, Barron, WI 54812-1478.

faqs.q: Who pays the Wisconsin real estate transfer fee in Barron County?
faqs.a: The seller. The fee is 30 cents for each $100 of value and is collected when the deed is recorded. Inheritance transfers, foreclosure deeds and certain family transfers for nominal consideration are exempt.

faqs.q: What if my lottery credit is missing from my Barron County tax bill?
faqs.a: File a late claim with your town, village or city treasurer by January 31. The credit applies only to an owner-occupied primary residence, and the Treasurer's Office can answer eligibility questions.
